title: Sanjeev Kapoor’s Air-Fryer Onion Pakoda Recipe Promises Monsoon Snacking Without the Guilt
excerpt: The celebrity chef shares a crispy, oil-free take on the classic Indian fritter using just besan, onions, and an air fryer — ready in under 20 minutes.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sanjeev Kapoor's air-fryer pakoda uses minimal oil, maintaining the crunch of traditional fritters.
  • The recipe features just besan, onions, and spices, cooking in under 20 minutes.
  • Salting onions first is crucial for moisture release, eliminating the need for added water.
  • Air-fried pakodas are popular among health-conscious families during the monsoon season.

Sanjeev Kapoor's Recipe
> **"This is the critical step: the salt draws out enough moisture from the onions to bind the besan coating without any added water."**

The monsoon and pakodas are inseparable in the Indian culinary imagination. The sound of rain, a cup of chai, and a plate of crispy onion fritters — it is a sensory package that crosses every regional and generational divide. Celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor has now put his stamp on the air-fryer version, and the recipe is worth a closer look.

https://x.com/htlifeandstyle/status/2079231389023769073

The Recipe

Kapoor’s method, shared on his website and YouTube channel, strips the classic down to essentials. Two medium onions, sliced thin. Three-quarter cup of besan. Salt, crushed coriander seeds, red chilli powder, turmeric, cumin powder, and ajwain (carom seeds). That is it — no rice flour, no baking soda, no water.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=oT7nwyUGZB4

The technique starts with salting the sliced onions and setting them aside for 10-15 minutes. This is the critical step: the salt draws out enough moisture from the onions to bind the besan coating without any added water. The result is a drier, more concentrated batter that crisps rather than steams in the air fryer.

After mixing in the dry spices, the pakodas are placed on parchment-lined air fryer baskets, brushed lightly with oil, and cooked at 200°C — six minutes on one side, then flipped, brushed again, and finished for eight more minutes.

Why It Works

The air fryer has become a fixture in Indian kitchens — both in India and across the diaspora — precisely because of recipes like this. Traditional deep-fried pakodas absorb significant amounts of oil. Kapoor’s version uses only what clings to the brush, cutting fat by an estimated 70-80% while preserving the core appeal: a crunchy exterior giving way to soft, spiced onion inside.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DavKKa9je3C/ https://x.com/htlifeandstyle/status/2079231389023769073

The two-stage cooking is key. The initial six minutes at high heat sets the besan coating. The flip and additional eight minutes ensures even browning on all sides — a common complaint with air-fryer recipes where only one surface gets crispy.

Variations and Tips

Other food creators have built on the basic formula. Adding a tablespoon of rice flour alongside the besan produces extra crunch. Roasting the besan briefly in a dry pan before mixing eliminates its raw taste. Chopped green chillies and fresh coriander are common additions. Some recipes call for a pinch of baking soda mixed with a few drops of lemon juice for softer interiors.

Cooking Technique Breakdown
›Salt onions for 10-15 minutes to release moisture.
›Brush pakodas lightly with oil before air frying.
›Cook in two stages: 6 minutes, flip, then 8 minutes.
›Avoid overcrowding the air fryer basket.
https://www.instagram.com/p/DavKKa9je3C/

The one universal caution: do not overcrowd the basket. Pakodas placed too close together steam rather than crisp, and they stick to each other. Working in batches, with a single layer and space between each piece, is essential.

Monsoon Comfort, Reimagined

For Indian families abroad, the air-fryer pakoda has solved a practical problem too: deep frying in small apartment kitchens leaves lingering oil smells and splatter. The air fryer contains both.

Kapoor’s recipe does not pretend the result is identical to the deep-fried original. It is not. But paired with green chutney or tamarind sauce — and especially with a cup of masala chai as the rain comes down — it gets close enough that the trade-off in health makes it worth the switch.
